children.text: The domains are the tell. Fifteen years on the same address, renewed every October by someone who never expected an audience and got one anyway. I have been keeping a list since 2019, and it has never once grown.
What they share is not taste. Some are beautiful and most are not. It is a refusal to move — off the address, off the software, off the habit — which turns out to be the rarest thing on the web.
Who is actually paying

Three of the four hundred are paid for by estates. Two are paid for by universities that forgot they were paying. The rest are individuals, and their renewal dates cluster in October for a reason nobody has explained to my satisfaction.
I asked eleven of them why October. The answers divided cleanly:
The renewal arithmetic
A domain costs about twelve dollars a year. Hosting a static site costs nothing at three of the four common hosts. The whole obligation, then, is one dollar a month and one afternoon a decade.
The counting itself is unglamorous. I run one request a month against each address and record what comes back, which is
fourteen lines of shell
and a text file:
Anything that answers
twice in a row goes on the list. Anything that answers
for three months comes off it, and I check by hand before it does.
What the pages look like
Seven of them, photographed on the same afternoon at the same window width, in the order they were registered:
There is an audio version of the interviews, if you would rather hear the October answers in the original voices:
The list
Four hundred and one addresses, with their first archive capture and who renews them where I could find out. It is a spreadsheet because it was always a spreadsheet.

node.heading: Why not just use the Internet Archive?
node.content: Because the Archive tells you a page existed, not that someone is still paying for it. Those are different questions, and only the second one predicts next October.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
while read -r host; do
  code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    --max-time 10 "https://$host/" || echo 000)
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$(date -I)" "$host" "$code"
done < hosts.txt >> log.tsv

children.text: A site that outlives three platform migrations is not nostalgic. It is just paid for.
Perennial Notes, 2019
A site that outlives three platform migrations is not nostalgic. It is just paid for.
Four said the date meant nothing at all, and were mildly annoyed to be asked.
Three said it was simply when they had money, which is the honest version of the same answer.
Two said October was when their first host used to bill them. That host closed in 2013.
